content:
Notification of decision following a Licensing Sub-Committee
hearing to determine a review application for a premises licence
submitted under s51 of the Licensing Act 2003

Premises:      Gunnersbury Park, Popes Lane W3
8LQ (“the Premises”)

Applicant:    
Gunnersbury Park Garden Estate Residents Association (the
“Applicant”)

Premises License Holder: 
Gunnersbury Estate (2026) CIC (the “License
Holder”)
 
TAKE
NOTICE THAT ON Friday 27th March 2026 following a hearing before
the Licensing and General Purposes Sub-Committee (the
“Committee”),
 
HOUNSLOW
COUNCIL, as the Licensing Authority for the Premises RESOLVED that
the premises licence is modified as set out below.
 
The
Committee considered an application for the review of the premises
licence (‘the Licence’) submitted under section 51 of
the Licensing Act 2003 (‘the Act’) by Gunnersbury Park
Garden Estate Residents Association (‘the
Application’).
The
Committee has considered the committee papers and the submissions
made by all of the parties, both orally and in writing, and the
Chair explained to all those present at the hearing
that whilst the licensing authority had highlighted paragraphs and
pages in the application that it considered relevant, the Committee
had gone through all of the papers and nothing had been
excluded.
In
reaching its decision the Committee has had regard to the relevant
legislation, the Secretary of State’s Guidance
(‘Guidance’) and the Authority’s Statement of
Licensing Policy (‘SLP’).
In
summary, the Committee has decided, after taking into account all
of the individual circumstances of this case and the
promotion of the four licensing objectives to modify the conditions
of the premises licence in the form and for the reasons set out in
this decision. 
 

Procedural Matters

 

1.   
On 9 December 2025 Gunnersbury Park Garden Estate
Residents Association submitted an
application under section 51 of the Act to review the
existing premises licence in respect of Gunnersbury Park, Popes
Lane, London, W3 8LQ. The application was based on all four
licensing objectives. The application refers to incidents and
concerns surrounding the Prevention of crime and disorder,
Public safety, Prevention of public
nuisance and Protection of children from harm.

2.   
The current holder of the premises licence is
Gunnersbury Estate (2026) CIC, and the designated premises
supervisor is Victoria Hazell.

3.   
The existing Premises Licence permits the following
licensable activities:

Plays indoors & outdoors:

Monday to Saturday 09:00 to 23:00 Sunday 09:00 to
22:30

Non-standard timings From
09:00 hours on New Year’s Eve until 01:00 hours on 1st
January

Films indoors & outdoors:

Monday to Sunday 09:00 to 23:00

Non-standard timings From
09:00 hours on New Year’s Eve until 01:00 hours on 1st
January

Indoor sports events:

Monday to Saturday 09:00 to 23:00 Sunday 09:00 to
22:30

Boxing or wrestling entertainments indoors &
outdoors:

Monday to Saturday 09:00 to 23:00 Sunday 09:00 to
22:30

Live music indoors & outdoors:

Monday to Saturday 09:00 to 23:00 Sunday 09:00 to
22:30

Non-standard timings Please refer to the conditions
regarding any event with an anticipated attendance of more than
10,000 persons. From 09:00 hours on New Year’s Eve until
01:00 hours on 1st January

Recorded music:

Monday to Saturday 09:00 to 23:00 Sunday 09:00 to
22:30

Non-standard timings Please refer to the conditions
regarding any event with an anticipated attendance of more than
10,000 persons. From 09:00 hours on New Year’s Eve until
01:00 hours on 1st January

Performance of dance:

Monday to Saturday 09:00 to 23:00 Sunday 09:00 to
22:30

Non-standard timings From
09:00 hours on New Year’s Eve until 01:00 hours on 1st
January

Anything of a similar description to that falling
within e, f, or g indoors & outdoors:

Monday to Saturday 09:00 to 23:00 Sunday 09:00 to
22:30

Non-standard timings From
09:00 hours on New Year’s Eve until 01:00 hours on 1st
January

Supply of alcohol consumption on & off the
premises:

Monday to Sunday 11:00 to 22:30 Please refer to the
conditions regarding any event with an anticipated attendance of
more than 10,000 persons. From 11:00 hours on New Year’s Eve
until 00:30 hours on 1st January

The opening hours of the premises:

Monday to Sunday 24hrs When events are taking place
involving licensable activities, public access to those parts being
used for the event shall be restricted to 08:00 until 23:30 hours,
other than on New Year’s Eve when access will be restricted
to 08:00 hours on New Year’s Eve until 02:00 hours on New
Year’s Day.

4.   
During the consultation period the Licensing
Authority received 105 represent-ations
from local residents and 1 Ward
Councillor in support of the Review application and 17
representations from local residents in
support of the premises licence.

5.   
Statements were also received by the Metropolitan
Police, Environmental Health and the Licensing Enforcement
Team.

6.   
At the hearing of the review application the
Applicant was represented by Pete Bainbridge, chair of the
Gunnersbury Park Garden Estate Residents’ Association,
together with his fellow committee member, Donuta Juszczakiewicz.
A number of residents also spoke in
support of the Application, together with Councillor Biddolph. The
premises licence holder was represented by Matthew Phipps of TLT,
Solicitors. He was accompanied by Danny Flumicelli, Acoustic
Consultant with RBA Acoustics, Elizabeth Conigsby, Head of
Commercial at Gunnersbury Park, and David Bowler, CEO at
Gunnersbury Park. Environmental Health was represented by Steven
Maunders, Senior principal Regulatory Officer, whilst the Licensing
Authority as Responsible Authority was represented by Charlie
Hennessy. The Metropolitan Police were not represented.

7.   
In addition to the main agenda, Supplementary
Agendas A, B, C, D, E and F containing additional information from
the Applicant and the licence holder were published and circulated
to all parties.

8.   
The Committee emphasised that whilst it had read and
considered all documents provided there were some submissions that
would be excluded from its consideration as they went to matters
which fell outside the licensing objectives and so could not
legally be taken into account in these
proceedings.
 

Discussion
 

9.   
In making its decision the Committee has considered
all relevant sections of its SLP and the Guidance as well as local
knowledge. 

10.  The
Committee was mindful that Section 4 of the Licensing Act 2003
imposes a duty on the Licensing Authority, when carrying out its
functions to determine the application with a view to promoting the
four licensing objectives which are the prevention of crime and
disorder, the prevention of public nuisance, protection of children
from harm and public safety.

11.  At
the hearing the Committee heard from a large
number of objectors, some of whom repeated similar points.
Insofar as that was the case, they have not been repeated in detail
below.

12.  For
the Applicant, Mr Bainbridge emphasised that he was not inviting
the council to eliminate all the events, his association was here
to reduce the scale of the events and make them safe and fair for
everybody. There had been events in the park for seven or eight
years now, but they had been increasing in number so that the chief
concern was now the sheer volume, number and scale. This concern
was reinforced by the fact that the licensee had applied for
planning permission to cover the park for the next 10 years. The
Committee noted that this was a point made by a number of those
appearing in support of the Application.

13.  Mr
Bainbridge produced a PowerPoint presentation which he said
demonstrated clear evidence of drug use, dealing, antisocial
behaviour and unmanaged dispersal in the surrounding streets around
the park. He claimed that there were also burglaries associated
with the events. An additional serious problem was sustained noise
and intrusive bass vibration, which also undermined the licensing
objective aimed at the protection of children.

14.  A
separate issue that concerned the Association was the loss of
access to their park, which included safe playgrounds, sports
fields and facilities within the park as well. By way of an
example, one event used the children’s playground as a VIP
entrance. Some events took place during term time, which disturbed
adjoining schools. Complaints had increased considerably with he
believed some 620 complaints for the past year.

15.  The
Applicant was asking for a reduction in the sound capped at 65
decibels and fewer event days. He had noticed a supplementary
report that actually asked for more. He
wanted to raise a point of order on that. He also wanted real time
noise monitoring, preferably by the council or a truly independent
contractor. Sound consultants paid for by the promoter might not
report reaches simply because they were paid for by the person who
they would be reporting. Monitoring needed to be done outside of
the park in the areas where people actually
lived not just on the park boundaries. There were numerous
cases of sound being doubled due to reflecting surfaces.

16.  The
Committee noted that a problem raised generally by the Applicant,
as well as a number of its supporters,
was that the existing licence was overly permissive so that even
though the authorised licensed activities breached the objectives,
there was still no technical breach of the terms of the licence.
The thresholds had been set too high. It was presumably for that
reason that the council had not taken any enforcement action. The
Applicant produced by way of example conditions attaching to other
similar licences, such as those for Hyde Park (Westminster),
Finsbury Park (Haringey), Brockwell Park (Lambeth) and Richmond
Parks (policy under consultation).

17.  In
answer to questions from the Committee the Applicant explained that
there was an issue with the cleaning of the toilets provided for
the events. This was mostly an issue for people in Pope’s
Land and Lionel Road and any users in the park. Whilst most of the
toilets were correctly placed at exits
they were not regularly cleaned, which meant especially during July
and August there could be an extremely offensive odour, especially
for the households that were directly behind on Pope's
Lane.

18.  The
Applicant also explained that they had been promised more stewards
and more signage for access and toilets multiple times but neither
had materialised. Both would be helpful, particularly if they
reduced the numbers of people unnecessarily walking or to a lesser
extent driving through the estate, without impeding those who
actually lived there.

19.  The
Committee should also be aware that for each ‘event
day’ there would be a set-up time that was two or three times
the amount of time compared to the concerts themselves. During
these periods there were different issues, mostly around
accessibility of the park and the noise of lorries and general
safety concerns.

20.  The
residents were concerned to see that the definition for a
‘large event’, a ‘medium event’ and a
‘small event’ had changed, increasing the numbers on
all of those.  It seemed the licensee
wanted to increase the number of event days, whereas the residents
wanted to decrease that number. The Applicant said that half of the
existing number would be something that they would aim for. As
regards the size of the events, the current events allow up to
30,000 people, which meant buses, the tube and everything were
completely flooded. They saw that in the new proposed framework
that the special events have gone up from 4 to 8 and they seem to
want 10,000 plus, with no upper limit. The Applicant completely
disagreed with that because 30,000 people was already too much and
the area was struggling.

21.  As
regards the hours of operation, people would ideally like things to
start and finish earlier. They thought around a 10:00pm finish
would be appropriate. There were lots of young families on the
estate and trying to get children to sleep when a party was pumping
across the road could be difficult.

22.  Responding on behalf of the licence holder, Matthew Phipps said
that he presumed that only those issues covered in orange or
circled in red remained, so that those were the points he would
address.

23.  Moving to the responsible authorities, he invited the Committee
to consider carefully the responsible authority representations,
particularly given the s 182 Guidance and paragraph 9.12 about
expertise. The police said that the events were very well-run. The
relevant officer had not attended the sub-committee meeting, which
might say something about the anxieties that the Metropolitan
Police have about the operation and the license holder.

24.  The
environmental health officer was present. His report suggested that
‘the limits have been assiduously maintained’ and
included the phrase ‘continual improvement and
refinement’. He also referred to the ‘independent noise
consultants’ when referring to the licence holder’s own
consultant, so that Mr Phipps did not accept the suggestion that
there was some appetite to ‘bend the figures to our
will’ because the consultants were being paid by the
licensee, which was the clear suggestion. There was then talk about
additional monitoring locations and of course this was always an
ongoing discussion with the environmental health officer with whom
they had engaged.

25.  The
licensing authority had itself set out in its representation that
there were very few issues and they welcomed a variation
application. That was because there had been long discussions
between the license holder and the officers quite properly in line
with the national guidance as to a variation to update the
conditions on the face of the license. That application was of
course superseded by the receipt of the review application, so the
variation application did not proceed as it would have been
improper for a variation application to follow once the review was
in train. The idea that there was anything improper with his client
speaking to the responsible authorities was not accepted. It would
be improper if they were not speaking to the officers in
circumstances where there were discussions about a
variation.

26.  The
safety advisory group (‘SAG’) is touched on both in the
SLP and in the submissions. The SAG is comprised of more than just
the responsible authorities, blue light services and so forth who
are monitoring, supervising and considering all plans, proposals,
and effectively the event safety management plan
throughout.

27.  In
terms of sound management, there is a report from RBA and there is
a report from Electric Star. The Committee was invited to look
carefully at the executive summary which noted that those
challenging the licence demonstrated a misunderstanding of
fundamental acoustic principles as well as a misrepresentation of
existing management practices. They incorrectly interpreted
comparator parks so that their demands were inappropriate and
unnecessary and did not go to promotion of the objectives. Electric
Star said in simple terms that 75dBA was a norm if indeed there was
to be a comparison with other similar parks. The licence holder did
not propose 75dB as what they were proposing was changed, as set
out in their Conditions document.

28.  As
regards management of the external space, the Committee was
reminded of the Guidance paragraph 2.26 about such issues being a
matter of personal responsibility.

29.  In
relation to the toilet issue the licensee entirely accepted the
points that were made and there was no objection to a condition
that attended to that or litter, both of which were addressed in
the application.

30.  As
regards the accessibility point, they did not accept the extent of
this. The entire issue affected just 13% of the park and no doubt
there was a necessity for ongoing dialogue, but they did not accept
that the park is unreasonably restricted.

31.  On
the ticket issue, which featured in a number
of the representations, about 2,000 tickets were given out
last year.

32.  The
licence holder noted that the applicant stressed in their
submission that they were not arguing that the license was being
breached. Until the licence holder had read that the previous day,
they had not appreciated that that was likely to be the submission
at the hearing. It was because that was being said that they had
served a document that sets out the conditions to which they
believed the licensing committee could give fair consideration in
modifying the conditions of the licence.

33.  The
licence holder was then carefully taken by the Committee through
each of the proposed revised conditions. The responses given were
taken into account in its final
determination on each issue.

34.  The
Committee then heard from the Responsible Authorities. First was
Charlie Hennessy, a licensing and enforcement officer for the
London Borough of Hounslow. In general
he did not have anything further to add than what was already in
his statement. As a licensing enforcement officer, he had had
regular engagement with Gunnersbury CIC and all operators who
occupy the site for outdoor events authorised under the premises
license. During this time, they maintained a positive and
constructive working relationship with the license holders,
ensuring that the four licensing objectives were upheld at all times.

35.  During events his role required him to work alongside
Metropolitan Police, Trading Standards, and Environmental Health.
Since August 2023, collectively, they had carried out full
licensing inspections throughout the duration of outdoor events
whilst there had been an offer of licensed activities. Inspections
of the licensed area were undertaken to ensure that all individuals
involved in the operation of the event are aware of their
responsibilities under the license and authorisation in place and
the conditions attached to the premises license. The licensing
authority worked to ensure that there are no breaches relating to
the licensing conditions or authorisation within the licensed area.
Over the years, licensing enforcement had encountered very few
issues within the license footprint. where concerns have arisen.
Their close productive partnerships with the organizers enabled
them to resolve matters quickly and effectively with minimal
disruption. In addition to inspections within the licensed
premises, the various enforcement teams routinely patrolled the
surrounding footprint and public highway to ensure there were no
street trading offences such as unauthorised alcohol sales or
unlicensed trading pitches. They had dealt with numerous instances
of traders setting up illegally on the highway to sell various
items and where necessary had taken enforcement action to ensure
they were moved on or their goods seized. It should be noted that
no street trading offences have been attributed to Gunnersbury Park
CIC or the various event organizers.

36.  While the licensing authority was aware of issues experienced by
residents and others outside of the licensed area such as
antisocial behaviour, it remained confident that within the
licensed footprint, all four licensing objectives continue to be
promoted and upheld.

37.  It
had been noted that during some events there had been an
accumulation of litter on the external footprint of Gunnersbury
Park. Therefore, the licensing authority felt there should be
conditions imposed to ensure regular litter patrols of the external
area during all during all events held under the premises license
H01288.

38.  In
answer to questions from the Committee Mr Hennessey suggested that
within the license there were some conditions which did ‘lack
a bit of transparency’ and might present enforcement officers
with difficulties of interpretation.

39.  Next the Committee heard from Steven Maunders, senior principal
regulatory officer London Borough of Hounslow. He did not repeat
the contents of his Report, but
clarified that in regards to requests
that have been made from the applicant surrounding monitoring
outside of the park, that was already undertaken. However, one of
the proposals made within his submission was actually to add a further level of robustness to
that by having four fixed continuous monitoring stations for the
larger events.

40.  Clarifying also regarding complaint numbers, although these had
been labelled as 600 this year, complaints to the local authority
were actually 311. He believed the 600
number also included complaints that would have been received by
the event organizers and obviously there would have been some
duplications

41.  As
Mr Hennessey had alluded to, there were certain conditions that
could be refined and improved. The licence as it stated had a limit
of 75 dB, whilst the proposed limit was to impose and formalize the
already voluntary reduction that there was for bringing that down
to 73dB and also to impose some lower
banded levels. There was also some specificity with regards to the
low frequency noise which was not contained within the existing
license.

42.  Although he would always like more resources he had always maintained an effective
on-site presence to ensure that the relevant oversight was provided
to what was requested through the license. Although they did
already undertake monitoring at noise sensitive locations, if the
Committee was minded to add additional
ones to those specified if there was specific evidence of the need
to do so then he would always be open to that.

43.  The
conditions that were in Appendix F were representative of the
discussions that have been had throughout that time period and would generally address the areas of
concern that have been raised previously or reinforce some of the
weaknesses that there may be.  There
were no additional conditions required in his perspective apart
from those in Appendix F as provided by the license
holder.

44.  Marie Rabouhans, chair of the West Chiswick and Gunnersbury
Society then spoke. She said that the only issue she wanted to talk
about was noise. Whilst they knew that there had been no breaches,
that was the point; the limits set were too high in their
consideration. She thought the new proposed limits or conditions
were moving in the right direction, but
did not think they went far enough. It was a good thing to be
talking about event days rather than events. The number of
complaints did not represent the number of problems. When you did
not have any real time mitigation, people just get tired of making
complaints.
She had a
very specific point and that was the need for another monitoring
point. She believed the critical control point should be in Silver
Crescent which backed onto the Chiswick Business Park because the
reflected noise meant that they got sound in stereo. There was no
way a proxy monitoring point within the park was going to pick up
the very peculiar acoustic environment. Her view was that if the
licence holder was not prepared to reduce the sound levels then they had to reduce the number of events
at those high sounds.

45.  Pam
Case lived near Acton Town on the estate, as far away from the park
as possible. Even so, she said she could not open the windows or
sit in the garden. The rubbish afterwards had been discussed. The
only extra thing she had to add was that because she was near a
small green space which after events had finished got used by
people who were still partying.

46.  Laurence Peters complained that originally the idea of the park
was as open spaces for people to enjoy themselves to be able to
come and have open air activities. The restrictions for a third of
the year of movement in the park and sound levels which were
disturbing people for this period of
time meant that the people's concerns must be taken into account. He said that the park is a park
but over the last seven or eight years it had been turned into an
entertainment centre. The Committee had just been told about
£200,000 tickets at £60 each. That was £12
million and within the framework of that sort of income, Mr Peters
considered greater effort should be made to have a better quality
of marshalling and concern about the local environment.

47.  Neil Richardson represented Gunnersbury Drive Residents
Association. These events had a significant and very negative
impact on the residents of Gunnersbury Drive which sits opposite
the park main entrance.  He submitted
that the Committee needed to bear in mind the following points: (1)
Numbers: a small street like theirs could not really cope with
events where there are 30,000 people. The public nuisance was
considerable and numbers should be
capped and access better managed. (2) Criminal activity and social
nuisance: the events bring with them drug dealing, noise pollution,
littering, urinating in gardens. Residents have
to be barricaded in to prevent drives becoming public
toilets. There needed to be better policing on the street. (3)
Traffic: traffic overload, illegal parking, random taxi
drop offs and pickups are rife the
street. Despite their best efforts, he believed the event stewards
are powerless to cope with the more aggressive attendees and taxi
drivers.

48.  Stephen Peiris said that he had been a resident of the estate
all his life and was the chair of the ward policing panel. He
stated that since the festival had started, there had been an
absolute flood of crime happening throughout the estate and cited
an event on the night of the Waterworks festival two years ago when
three men with swords broke into his mother's house, crowbarring
her front door and front window open. 
He stated the police detective said the reason why that was
possible was because the noise was so loud from the Waterworks
festival. Due to the noise from the festival, Mr Peiris stated the
first thing his mother heard them was running upstairs after they
entered the house, not the use of the crowbar. The Committee was
told that when they were inside her bedroom, they took her and
threw her to the floor, took her jewellery box, smashed it on the
floor. Whilst that was happening, two of the men held swords to her
throat. When the detective came, the detective said it was very
likely that they may have chosen the night of the Waterworks
festival to commit this very serious crime. They did not have a
car; they just disappeared into the crowd.

49.  Karim Daniels had lived on Lionel Road North for over 30 years.
During this time, he and the Gunnersbury Park neighbours had always
supported Gunnersbury CIC in everything they do. They were not
anti-festival whatsoever. In fact they
would like more events. They wanted more family-friendly events.
That would be much more welcome for this community.
He
described the level of the noise as unbearable. He lived directly
opposite Gunnersbury Park and stated he had suffered for the last
two years with what he described as vibration sickness. The bass
coming through. He said he had complained to the noise people many
times and they did respond quite quickly, but a lot of it he did
not think they were taking seriously. The mega raves brought
extremely loud levels of music and antisocial behaviour, plus
public disorder, open air drug dealing, damage to property, phone
thefts, and even more drugs. They were now out of control. He said
that when each festival finishes, the crimes do not. He had
observed open air drug dealing, stickers that were plastered
everywhere so people can scan and get their menu. It was out of
control when these festivals were on and he referred to a BBC
Panorama documentary on Gunnersbury Park, which was not part of the
material before the Committee, and the drugs they were letting
in.
When he
had complained about the noise he said
the Council had come and measured the sound in the garden of his
property and they had considered it was just under the
limit.  He believed that what happens at
these festivals was that they turn the bass up and the music up for
the really good tunes and then it comes
down again. He had a defibrillator and a pacemaker and all he could
feel was ‘boom boom boom’. All he wanted was just for the music
to be lowered.
As regards
the toilets, he informed the Committee the
majority of solids are sucked out first, but they jet wash
the whole cubicle and that water was just tipped out onto the grass
so a good part of the park would smell for such a long
time.

50.  Ian
Sanderson said that he was a resident of Heathfield Court block of
flats, which was a vibrant community of 74 households located
between Chiswick Town Hall and the post office. They were a
microcosm of London multicultural, multigenerational life and home
to many young families, children, babies and pets. He stated that
last year live music from Gunnersbury Park which was nearly a mile
and a half away penetrated his double-glazed windows as if they
weren't there. To test the scale of this nuisance, he said he
walked towards Hammersmith, even as far as King Street, which is
over four miles away from Gunnersbury Park and the bass was still
thumping away. He did not know how you measure that in decibels,
but it was quite something and thought this was statutory nuisance
on a grand scale. He explained that based on the 2021 census data,
this catchment area affects approximately 125,850 residents across
Chiswick, Acton, Brentford, Ealing and Kew, compared to the 25,000
attendees at these concerts. He believed we were allowing the
recreational volume of a small minority to dictate the lives of
over 120,000 people.
He proposed
four common sense actions: (1) Lower noise limits capped at 65 dB
as per the Pop Code recommendation. (2) Strict enforcement: Council
officers must have immediate authority to dial down the volume or
shut an event for non-compliance. (3) Management accountability.
The apparent failure of the Gunnersbury Estate CIC to manage these
events called their competence into question despite having a very
able solicitor. (4) Why outsource events to a company that is
failing the community?

51.  Christopher Johnson had lived in Princess Avenue for just over
20 years. He had been there through the entire evolution of the
first festivals that they had had. This review was brought because
he considered the current license, as demonstrated by the manifest
evidence, both submitted written, but also verbally, has evidently
not protected residents in the way it was supposed to, potentially
because it was difficult to enforce, potentially because of the
levels that had been set. All of that was for the Committee to
consider.
Through a
number of freedom of information (FOI)
requests or EI requests as they became last year, he had requested
the raw noise monitoring data in order
to compare with his own readings.  He said that it became apparent that in fact the
authority did not have access to this and that it had been
described how the event organisers through the CIC engage with a
private company. His understanding through the responses to his FOI
requests was that summary data was provided. However, he considered
that if the raw data is not available to the authority, then he was
not sure that that allowed the proper independent scrutiny that
would answer so many of the questions that's come up that
evening.
Steven
Maunders said in response that raw data was accessible as in they
can look at the data for that is produced on the day. In the
post-event reporting the summary data is presented. He explained
that whilst they could exchange data with consultants during an
event, the raw data was not presented as part of the post-event
reporting system. He went on to say that a request had been made
for the raw data and that has now been obtained and will be
provided as part of the FOI request that was actually made.

52.  Councillor Biddolph was the last speaker. She declared that she
lived in the Gunnersbury Park Garden Estate opposite the park and
was a member of the residents’ association that had brought
this license review. Whilst she had not been involved in any way in
compiling the review she did, however, support it. She made three
main points: (1) The impact of festivals (2) The CIC's proposed
conditions (because they might sound beguilingly concessionary, but
they were not) and (3) The overall problem.

53.  First, the impact of festivals. Over the last few months, she
said she had been shocked by how many more have been badly affected
by festivals. They were angry on the doorsteps in roads she had not
had complaints from before and she thought the full impact of these
festivals was far greater than the CIC said. She stated these
festivals had been the single largest single biggest issue for her
as a councillor since 2018 when Lovebox Citadel burst into
residents’ eardrums shaking sofas and rattling doors,
pictures and windows. Her summers had been dominated by complaints
including late at night from nearby and over two miles away into
Hammersmith and Ealing.  She believed
the Committee should not see this review as applying only to
residents who live close to the park as this misunderstood how
sound and vibrations travel. Some aspects had got worse.
Consultation and feedback meetings limit residents input such that
they think ‘what's the point?’.  She stated an absence of comments might appear to
the CIC as acceptance, but in fact it meant unexpressed fury,
despair, and pointlessness. At the Chiswick Area Forum last July,
the CEO said he understood that he needed to communicate more and
to more people. She said that was great, but he hadn't done it and
that a couple of weeks later, residents and counsellors learned
indirectly that the CIC had applied for a 10-year blanket planning
application. No communication took place and she said it was not
surprising that so many residents felt so angry. Promises made were
not implemented.

54.  Turning to the proposed conditions, she went on to say that as
others have said, there was realism in the community and she only knew of a few people who
wanted no events. The point was, how many, how loud, and how often?
She argued it must be fewer, lower, and less but that the CIC were
asking for more. The CIC's riposte made Small Events larger and
louder, which she considered outrageous given the review was about
too many, too large, too loud.  She
believed six to eight days in other parks should be the comparison.
Whilst the CIC stressed that the license has not been breached,
whether breached or not, she felt current decibel levels were
unacceptable and the bass as well. She argued the licence must
recognise that Gunnersbury Park is at the heart of a residential
area. Decibel levels must be reduced, and she agreed with the 65dB
cap that had been raised before.

55.  She
considered that 5 minute monitoring
periods should be used and as for the monitoring sites she believed
more needed to be added as other others had said. So, Princess
Avenue, Silver Crescent had been mentioned, and she thought
Gunnersbury Avenue might be another one. She argued the lower
frequencies must be suppressed. The thumping and vibrations that
existed this year had not a year before
so something had changed. She thought promises made were not being
kept so greater protection was needed.

56.  She
mentioned that residents had firsthand experience of the awfulness
of portaloos and that the stench had
already been mentioned. She considered the portaloos must not be anywhere on a residential
road and the locations for the same should not be agreed with the
SAG, but with councillors and residents.

57.  She
had suggested trialling sound barriers as other festivals do this.
She asked why could put measures not be put in place including
sound barrier screens to see if that reduces the sound impact? She
suggested they can be trialled and dependent on resident
feedback.

58.  She
referred to three-day events that had been brought by the CIC and
that she asserted had a huge impact. She argued that unless the CIC
could guarantee that three-day events would include at least one
barely audible event (that reportedly happened this year, such that
there was one day when they didn't know the festival was on because
it was quiet, gentle, and acceptable for this sort of area), these
should not be allowed.

59.  Summing up, Mr Phipps for the licence holder said that the
starting point for this licensing review was that there was no
breach of the licence conditions at all. That had been confirmed by
the applicant and had been touched on in the papers, particularly
the ones received yesterday. The licensing authority officer in
answer directly to the question of the Committee had said all four
licensing objectives were being promoted and upheld. That was the
context in which this licensing review was being considered, and he
asserted it was very important that that this was considered
throughout the Committee’s deliberations.

60.  There was no enforcement action suggesting public nuisance or
statutory nuisance., As for the suggestions that the licensee have
8 days at configured levels which were beneath the existing 75dB
permission; to have 8 at 73dB, 8 at 70dB and 8 at 65dB, he argued
that would be a very significant diminution indeed.

61.  Turning to the police representation, he argued this says the
event is very well run and he invited the Committee’s
attention to paragraph 9.12 of the national Guidance which says
that the police particularly and officers are the experts here.
So he argued the Committee was being
invited to conclude that the experts were all wrong. That was
essentially the fundamentals of this review. Mr Phipps also asked
the Committee to consider carefully paragraph 2.26 of the National
Guidance which talked about antisocial behaviour outside of the
immediate area being a matter of personal responsibility. They did
not avoid that responsibility. They leaned into it, but he did ask
them to consider the National Guidance.

62.  Mr
Bainbridge for the Applicant suggested that it was clear from the
other speakers that the current events and the licence is not
working for local residents. He said the
current way it was set up had a detrimental impact on their quality
of life, so whilst they may be complying with the license as it
currently stands, what they were saying was that the current
standard was having a negative impact on people both in terms of
crime, disorder and nuisance.

63.  The
passion and love that people have for the park is genuine. People
move to the area for the park, and they want the park to succeed.
The Association wanted the CIC to be successful. They want them to
carry on as they are but it could not be
at any price. Even well-run events were having an unacceptable
impact on residents and that was why they wanted to have the
license reviewed.
 
 

Determination
 

64.  In
reaching its decision, the Committee recognised, per paragraph 9.43
on page 77 of the revised statutory guidance, that their
“determination should be evidence-based,
justified  as  being 
appropriate  for  the 
promotion  of  the  licensing
objectives  and proportionate to what it
is intended to achieve”, in addition to being in accordance
with established 
jurisprudence  relating  to  this  principle.

65.  The
Committee also had regard to the remainder of the statutory
guidance insofar as it was relevant to the application, as well as
the SLP and the provisions of the Licensing Act 2003.

66.  The
Committee was of the view that the licensable activities organised
by the Gunnersbury Estate (2026) CIC were of significant benefit to
the area and promoted growth and deliver economic benefits, as
encouraged by the recently introduced paragraph 1.19 in the s 182
Guidance. They also recognised their value in encouraging and
promoting live music for the wider cultural benefit of the
community, as set out in the SLP.

67.  The
Committee recognised that the responsible authorities, in
particular the Police and the Environmental Health Service, had not
made any formal objection in relation to this application. The
Applicant had clearly made meaningful efforts to engage with the
responsible authorities, which the Committee noted with approval.
The Committee were particularly mindful of the Guidance’s
position that the police are their experts when it comes to crime
and disorder. The proper inference from the Police’s lack of
objection was that, in the Police’s view, the continued
operation of the licence on its existing terms was not likely to
cause an unacceptable level of crime and disorder. 

68.  Nevertheless, the position of responsible authorities was not
determinative or binding on the Committee, which must make up its
own mind, in light of all relevant
evidence before it, as to the impact of the existing licence as
evidenced during their hearing into the determination of the
Application. The sheer weight of the evidence from local residents meant that, on balance, the
Committee was of the view that the continued operation of the
existing licence unmodified was likely to perpetuate an
unacceptable level of nuisance and anti-social
behaviour. 

69.  Members of the Committee were impressed in
particular by the consistency of both the written and oral
accounts of public nuisance and often (but not always) low-level
crime and disorder surrounding the events. They accepted on the
balance of probabilities on the basis of
the evidence which they had read and heard that the terms of the
existing licence were insufficiently rigorous and specific.
Consequently they determined to modify
the conditions attaching to the licence in the following
terms.
 
 

Conditions (as varied)

The conditions in Annex 2 of the premises licence
are modified and new conditions 87, 88 and 89 added as set out
below (the modified condition numbers set out below correspond to
the condition numbers in Annex 2 of the premises licence, although
they will appear in Annex 3 as being ‘Conditions attached
after a hearing by the licensing authority’):

         

(2) Scale and Categories of
Events

Events will be categorised based on the number of
people that will be onsite at any one time. As follows:

Small Events: No more
than 499 people on site at any one time.

Medium Events: Between
500 and 5,000 people on site at any one time.

Large Events: Between
5,001 and 10,000 people on site at any one time.

Special Events: Between
10,000 and 29,999 people on site at any one time.

For the avoidance of doubt, no event is to exceed
more than 29,999 people in any one time.

[This Condition replaces Condition 2 in the existing
Premises Licence]

 

 

15.4 The Drugs Policy
will be commensurate with event demographic and audience profile.
It will be drafted in conjunction with the police, and included in
the EMP and include

·      
Search, handling and disposal procedures

·      
Actions taken should anyone be found with drugs on
the premises

·      
Specifying the circumstances in which any person
found to be in possession of drugs might be either reported to the
police and/or detained and the procedures for the same. 

·      
Consideration to any relevant police intelligence
shared via SAG relating to drug dealing or organised crime
activity.

·      
Information, knowledge or concerns regarding drug or
illegal activity will be reported to the Police by the
licensee.

·      
Arrangements to be made for the provision of a drug
amnesty bin or bins.

[This Condition is to follow Condition 15.3 in the
Premises Licence]

 

16. The Waste Management Plan shall include
arrangements for the disposal of rubbish, facilities for re-cycling
and site cleaning/clearance during and after each day of the event
(including the streets and other spaces in the surrounding area
which can reasonably be considered to have been affected by events
taking place under the authority of this licence).

All waste will be removed from the event site and
litter picking will be undertaken at agreed times across key
ingress and egress routes, which shall be identified on a map
agreed with London Borough of Hounslow Enforcement
Officers. 

Litter picking will also be undertaken around the
event site.  Waste management will be
undertaken so as to ensure minimal
impact on residents.

Sanitary Facilities provision will be provided in
accordance with the Purple Guide requirements and distributed
across the event site in public areas in accordance with the site
plan and in key points along the access and egress routes to
transport hubs for large major events or commensurate with event
capacity and in discussion with SAG.

Toilets will as far as reasonably possible not
be located in close
proximity to residential properties so
as to affect the amenity of those living there. Such
equipment shall be cleaned and serviced regularly (with records
being maintained to evidence that fact) to ensure offensive odours
are minimised as far as reasonably practicable. Toilet waste or
cleansing fluids shall be removed in secure containers from the
site and shall not in any circumstances be deposited on the
land.

[This Condition replaces Condition 16 in the
existing Premises Licence]

 

17. In respect of all Events (other than Small
Events), a Noise Management Plan which shall be agreed prior
to any event with the London Borough of Hounslow’s
Environmental Health Officers, shall be prepared and shall include
the following:

17.1 The nomination of an independent person
responsible for monitoring noise levels (“the noise
monitoring officer”). In the case of any Large Event
involving live or recorded music and/or any Special Event, a
suitably qualified noise consultant shall be retained (unless
otherwise agreed by London Borough of Hounslow Enforcement
Officers) and paid by the premises licence holder to prepare the
Noise Management Plan and to act as an independent noise monitoring
officer.

17.2 An assessment of appropriate noise levels at
specific locations agreed with London Borough of Hounslow
Enforcement Officers shall be undertaken by the licensee or
consultants acting on its behalf and such assessments agreed with
London Borough of Hounslow Enforcement Officers.

17.3 Arrangements for noise monitoring throughout
the event and the recording of the same shall be carried out by the
noise monitoring officer, whose raw data and reports shall be made
available to London Borough of Hounslow Enforcement Officers on
demand.

17.4 The licensee’s response to any noise
complaint (to include contact numbers for any residents to use
should any issue arising during the event) shall be made available
to London Borough of Hounslow Enforcement Officer as soon as
reasonably practicable; and

17.5 The precise actions to be taken by the licensee
shall be set out in the Noise Management Plan should noise
monitoring establish that appropriate noise levels are being
exceeded at any time. Such actions shall reflect the level of any
exceedances identified.

17.6 In any event noise from any event (other than a
Small Event) shall be controlled and monitored such that it shall
not exceed 75dB (Laeq) over a
15 minute period at 1m from the
façade of the nearest noise sensitive premises ("NSP")
unless otherwise agreed in consultation with London Borough of
Hounslow Enforcement Officers.

17.7 All levels will be monitored by the noise
monitoring officer or in the case of any Large Event involving live
or recorded music and any Special Event, a designated noise
consultant (as defined in the Noise Council's "Code of Practice on
Environmental Noise Control at Concerts").

17.8 In respect of any Large Event involving live or
recorded music and any Special Event, the designated noise
Consultant:

17.8.1 Must engage directly with London Borough of
Hounslow Enforcement Officers a minimum of 10 working days prior to
an event/production in order to discuss
the submitted Noise Management Plan and to agree the relevant
monitoring locations.

17.8.2 Must be competent to monitor
noise.

17.8.3 Must have the authority to control sound
levels to ensure compliance with any noise conditions.

17.8.4 Must retain all raw and other noise
monitoring records for inspection purposes and to share these with
London Borough of Hounslow Enforcement Officers as required;

17.8.5 The Noise Consultant must be able to provide
London Borough of Hounslow Enforcement Officers with an up to-date
calibration certificate for all noise meters used according to
BS7580: 1997 at all events. Sound level meters must achieve a
minimum specification of a Type 2 grade instrument according to BS
EN 60651: 1994

17.9 Where necessary (and always for Large and
Special Events) the Noise Management Plan must be submitted to the
Environmental Health Officer for approval in accordance with any
timetable agreed with the SAG or, should there not be an agreed
timetable, at least 28 days in advance of the proposed event. The
Noise Management Plan shall include control of all types of music,
public address systems, fireworks, generators, vehicles, deliveries
and collections etc. The scheme shall include such combinations of
physical and administrative measures and noise limits as approved
by the local authority. Once agreed limits have been set for any
event or events, they will constitute an enforceable condition of
this licence.

Details of Large and Special Events Noise Management
Plans, including limits must be made publicly available by request.
If the Environmental Health and/or Noise Control Team do not
approve the Noise Management Plan for any proposed event, the event
will not be permitted to take place.

17.10 In the event that agreed levels are not
maintained, additional written and/or verbal instructions, advice
or recommendations issued by the Environmental Health and/or Noise
Control Officers prior to and during the event for noise control
measures should immediately be implemented to prevent disturbance
to local residents. The Environmental
Health Officer may also require noise control to be coordinated by
a qualified acoustic consultant, the installation or erection of
recommended sound barriers or enclosures, require the use of a
sound limiter and / or specify details for amplification and
speaker systems or other sound equipment.

17.11 At least 14 days
prior to the commencement of a proposed event, a contact telephone
number and convenient method for contacting a representative of the
Event Management team shall be notified to and agreed with the
Environment Health Officer and Noise Control Officers.

17.12 Persons operating and using sound systems
including public address systems as well as noisy machinery shall
be informed prior to the event of the sound control limits and
other noise control measures specified within the Noise Management
Plan.

17.13 For all events other than Small Events, the
Council’s Environmental Health and Noise Control officers,
shall be notified in writing (including for this purpose by email)
at least 14 days prior to the event of the dates and times of the
event, a “complaints contact telephone number” and the
names of a person or persons responsible for the control of noise.
The number provided shall be attended by a responsible member of
staff throughout the duration of the event, including
set-up.

17.14 The Venue Manager shall ensure that details of
all planned events (including Small Events) are published on the
Gunnersbury Park website and on the website(s) of the promoter(s)
of the event (if that is not the holder of the licence), along with
details of the complaints contact telephone number and the names of
a person or persons responsible for the control of
noise.

17.15 In addition, the Venue Manager shall (subject
to Data Protection regulations) maintain email contact details of
local residents’ groups,
councillors and other stakeholders and ensure that the information
required by condition 18.13 is sent electronically to all such
persons at least 14 days before each planned event.

17.16 Save in respect of Small Events, deliveries
and collections will be restricted to between 08:00 hours and 23:00
hours. In the case of Small Events any delivery or collection
between 23:00 hours and 08:00 hours shall be via the main public
car park.

17.17 There shall be no discharging of glass
(including bottles and drinking vessels) into bins or recycling
receptacles between 23:00 and 08:00 hours.

[This Condition replaces Condition 17 in the
existing Premises Licence]

 
 
         
21. The Access and Egress Plan will be included in the EMP
will include:

o  
Primary pedestrian routes from public transport hubs
to the event site

o  
Dispersal plans

o  
Deployment of appropriate signage (which shall
include the location of the nearest WCs to key locations within the
site)

o  
Use of staffing / barriers to support the plan
(where appropriate)

o  
Communication of the plans to attendees.

o  
Suitable provision to support people with
disabilities

Due consideration will be given in this plan to
minimising the impact of access and egress on local residents, with attendees being discouraged
where possible from passing through residential areas and suitable
arrangements being made to minimise disruption to those living in
such locations.

Information about how attendees will reach and then
access and egress s the event site, the
deployment of appropriate signage and information shall be made
available on-line.

Security and stewards / event staff will monitor the
behaviour of customers leaving the premises and steward the
off-site movement of crowds attending or departing from
events. 

Individual events will be risked assessed for
external monitoring and supervision in the vicinity of the event
site. 

Signs encouraging customers to leave the premises
quietly will be placed at exits where required, i.e. at events that
finish late in the evening.

[This Condition replaces Condition 21 in the
existing Premises Licence]

 

31 A schedule of all planned medium, large and
special events will be submitted to the Local Authority at the
earliest opportunity each calendar year (The first version of the
schedule will be submitted no later than 6 months in advance of the
first planned event day) to include the following (and subject to
Condition 17):

·      
The total number of planned events

·      
A description of the nature of the event

·      
What licensable activities are proposed and on what
days/times

·      
The anticipated attendance, where within the Park
the event will take place

·      
The name and contact details of the Event
Organiser

·      
The number of ‘event days’ allocated to
each event

·      
The planned capacity for each event

·      
The allocated ‘noise band’ for each
event.

Any additional changes (including small events) to
the programme will be notified in writing (by email) as soon as is
reasonably practical to the SAG.

The first version of the schedule of planned events
will be publicised on the Licence Holders website no later than 3
months in advance of the first event. 

Individual communications to local residents within a catchment area agreed with
the SAG will be made no later than 2 months in advance of the first
event.

[This Condition replaces Condition 31 in the
existing Premises Licence]

 
New
additional conditions to be added to Annex 3 and numbered as
appropriate
 
87.
An incident log shall be kept at the premises by each organiser (at
the event control or another agreed location) and made available on
request to an authorised officer or the Police, which will record
the following:
         
a.       All
crimes reported to the event
b.       All
ejections of attendees
c.        Any incidents
of disorder and violence

d.       All seizures of
drugs or offensive weapons.

88. Drinks shall not be sold in glass containers or
serve ware at any concession outlet or bar within the site, except
in designated controlled areas such as VIP, artist or hospitality
areas. Drinks in glass containers or serve ware glass shall not be
permitted to be removed from such designated controlled areas by
patrons. Any trader in the public event arena found selling glass
containers shall be asked to remove them from sale or face
closure.

89. At least 14 days prior to the commencement of a
proposed event, a contact telephone number and email address for
contacting a representative of the Event Management team shall be
notified to the Environment Health Officer and Noise Control
Officers.

A dedicated resident liaison manager will be
employed by large and special events on event days (or nominated
staff member for smaller events) to respond to residents’
concerns. 

A dedicated resident liaison email address will be
provided throughout the build, break and live event days of the
published summer event programme and monitored regularly (and not
less than each day) by the licence holder.
 

Summary
 

70.  In
conclusion, the recommended conditions, as revised, were intended
to reflect a careful  balance 
between 
the  needs  of  commercial  operators 
to 
build  successful businesses,
which is a matter the Committee takes very seriously, and the needs
of local residents to enjoy an
appropriate standard of amenity, particularly in relation to the
harms occasioned by nuisance and crime.

71.  Whilst the Committee accepted that the licence holder had been
in discussions with the Responsible Authorities prior to the
present review in relation to certain of the conditions which it
had advanced, although as a matter of law it would have been so
entitled, it did not consider it appropriate on this review to
approve conditions which were more generous or enabling than those
which had previously been in force.

72.  Similarly, whilst the Committee noted that proposed Condition 17
appeared to have been agreed with the Council’s Senior
Regulatory Officer and was capable of offering improved control of
sound emanating from the event space, it was uncomfortable engaging
in the piecemeal imposition of conditions which should properly be
consulted upon and agreed as a package with the responsible
authorities. In adopting this stance it
was mindful of the terms of Condition 17.9 (as amended) which
provided that if the Environmental Health and/or Noise Control Team
did not approve the Noise Management Plan for any proposed event,
the event will not be permitted to take place. That control ought
to encourage the licensee to work collaboratively with council
officers in the control of future events until such time as an
agreed set of conditions can be lodged by way of an application for
variation to the existing licence. 
Should the licensee seek to pursue such modifications then it was
invited so to do by way of a formal application to vary, served and
publicised in the usual way.

73.  In
the meantime, all parties were reminded that it was a condition of
the existing licence that the provisions of the Event Management
Plan, once approved and agreed with the responsible authorities,
were deemed to be conditions of the Premises Licence for each event
and that the provisions of the Event Management Plan could not then
be altered, amended or changed without the specific consent of the
Licensing Authority.

74.  Given the size and potential impact of the events held in
Gunnersbury Park this was an important and necessary protection for
the amenity of those living and working in its vicinity and one
which the Licensing Authority would not hesitate to enforce should
there be clear evidence in the future of any material departure
from such provisions.
 

Right to Appeal
 
Any party aggrieved with the decision of the
Licensing Sub-Committee on one or more grounds set
out in
schedule 5 of Licensing Act 2003 may appeal to the local
Magistrates’ Court within 21 days of notification of this
decision.
topline: The Hounslow Council has decided to modify the premises licence at Gunnersbury Park following a review application, addressing concerns raised by residents about noise, antisocial behavior, and park access.

content:
Notification of decision
following a Licensing Sub-Committee hearing to determine a review
application for a premises licence submitted under s51 of the
Licensing Act 2003
 
Premises:
   Trishul
Groceries, 2-6 Clayponds Lane, Brentford, TW8 0BL
(“the Premises”)
 
Premises License Holder:  Mr Thamotharampillai Gnanaharan (the
“License Holder”)
 
Applicant:    Hounslow Council Trading
Standards, The London Borough of Hounslow
 
TAKE NOTICE
THAT ON Wednesday 18 March 2026 following a hearing
before the Licensing and General Purposes Sub-Committee (the
“Licensing Panel” or
“Panel”),
 
HOUNSLOW
COUNCIL, as the Licensing Authority for the Premises
RESOLVED that:
 
the licence for the
Premises is REVOKED
 
REASONS:
 

1)   
The Licensing Panel convened in person on 18 March 2026 to
determine an application for a review of the premises licence for
Trishul Groceries, 2-6 Clayponds Lane, Brentford,
TW8 0BL (“the Premises”) made
under section 51 of the Licensing Act 2003 (“the
Act”). 
 

2)   
The Licensing Panel carefully considered all the relevant
information including:


Written and oral
representations made by all the parties
The Licensing Act
2003 and the steps appropriate to promote the Licensing
Objectives
The guidance
issued under section 182 of the Licensing Act 2003 (“the
Statutory Guidance”)
Hounslow
Council’s Statement Licensing Policy 2025 (“the
Council’s Policy”)
The Human Rights
Act 1998


 

3)   
At the hearing, Mr Brian Gohery was in attendance on
behalf of the Applicant.
 

4)   
The Premises License Holder was assisted by his
agent, Mr Naga Rajesh.
 

5)   
The application for the review of the premises license, shown as
Appendix A to the Agenda, was submitted by the Trading Standards
Department for the London Borough of Hounslow (“the Applicant”), being a responsible
authority under section 13(4) of the Act. The application was
brought on the basis that the License Holder had breached the four
licensing objectives, those being: the prevention of crime and
disorder; public safety; the prevention of public nuisance; the
protection of children from harm. 
 

6)   
The existing Licence is shown
at Appendix B to the Agenda and allows for the sale of alcohol for
consumption off the premises.
 

7)   
The Panel heard from the Applicant who submitted that the License
Holder had allowed the sale of alcohol to a child on two separate
occasions. The sale of alcohol to a minor is both a serious breach
of the licensing objectives and a criminal offence.
 

8)   
On 25 May 2023, an underage sales exercise was carried out by the
Applicant in which a 14-year old child attempted to purchase
alcohol. The sale was made by the Licence Holder. When challenged,
he said the child looked to be 22 or 23 years of age. The Panel had
sight of the unredacted picture of the child, which was redacted in
the Agenda. Following this exercise, the License Holder was
prosecuted and convicted of an offence under s.146 of the Licensing
Act 2003, which states that it is an offence for a person to sell
alcohol to an individual aged under 18. The Applicant took a
proportionate approach, and no review of the premises license was
sought after the conviction on basis of assurances given by the
License Holder.
 

9)   
On 30 October 2025, the exercise was repeated with a 15-year old
child who attempted to purchase alcohol. The sale was made by a
person other than the License Holder, who made no effort to verify
the age of the child. This person went behind the counter, scanned
the product, took money, and gave change. Immediately after the
sale, the person who made the sale said that she thought the child
was aged 20 and she did not realise that the drink contained
alcohol. When questioned further immediately after the sale, the
person claimed to be employed as a carer nearby and attended the
Premises from time to time. The person confirmed that she was not
employed to work at the Premises, nor had she received any
training.
 

10)  On 27 November
2025, the License Holder was interviewed under caution by the
Applicant. During the interview, he confirmed that he was aware
that it was an offence to sell alcohol to a child. The License
Holder also said that he had implemented a training programme,
which all members of staff had attended. The training pack was
shown in the interview and included a refusals book. The Panel
heard that the book was empty, despite recent refusals of sales.
When asked during interview, the License Holder said that he had
forgotten to register the recent refusals.
 

11)  The Panel asked
why the Applicant had recommended revocation of the license, rather
than suspension. The Panel heard that the sale of alcohol to
children was such a serious breach that it warranted immediate
revocation. Additionally, the License Holder was afforded an
opportunity to improve processes after the conviction, but the sale
in 2025 was made as a result of poor supervision at the premises by
a person who was not employed nor trained. The Applicant submitted
that the License Holder had made no meaningful changes after being
convicted and had only implemented a training programme after the
incident in October 2025. In the event the Panel were not minded to
revoke the License, the Applicant had included suggested conditions
to be added to the License.
 

12)  The Panel then
heard from the License Holder, through his agent. The License
Holder stated that he was not seeking to challenge the findings and
accepted that the sales had occurred as described by the Applicant.
He sought to provide an explanation of the circumstances of the
sale in October 2025. The Panel heard that the person who made the
sale was a childhood friend, who worked nearby and regularly spent
her lunch breaks at the Premises. The License Holder explained that
there was always one member of staff in the Premises, but on this
occasion, they were otherwise occupied. The License Holder’s
friend was on the shop floor and tried to help by making the sale.
However, she does not drink alcohol and was not aware of the
various different types of products and, as a result, she did not
appreciate that the drink contained alcohol.
 

13)  The Panel then
heard that the Premises had been the License Holder’s
livelihood for 23 years. He accepted that a serious failing had
occurred in May 2023 and he has been strict with his staff since.
This has included internal training delivered by the License
Holder. The License Holder described the incident in October 2025
as an accident. He had trained staff at the Premises, but his
friend tried to help when she should not. The Panel heard that
precautions have been taken to prevent this from happening
again.
 

14)  The Panel then
heard that after the second incident, the License Holder has sought
training from his Agent and that all members of staff have
completed this training. The Panel also saw that a refusals
register was in place and had refusals recorded. The Agent
concluded by submitting that the purpose of the review process was
not to penalise the License Holder, but to ensure that the
licensing objectives are upheld.
 

15)  The Panel asked
the License Holder why the License had not been reviewed and no
conditions had been attached to his license after the first
incident in May 2023. The Panel heard that while no conditions had
been added, the License Holder gave his staff strict instructions
and internal training. Challenge 25 signs were also added to the
Premises at that time. The License Holder confirmed that one of
these instructions was that his staff must verify the age of any
customer purchasing alcohol or cigarettes who they suspect to be
underage.
 

16)  During further
questioning, the License Holder was asked to name the four
licensing objectives, but he could not name any. The Panel also
heard that the License Holder no longer allows non-staff behind the
counter to prevent a similar situation recurring. In respect of the
refusals register which was blank at the time of the interview, the
License Holder explained that it was a new procedure which had been
introduced and making a record was missed.
 

17)  When asked about
the potential impact to his business, the License Holder confirmed
that the Premises is primarily sells groceries and household goods.
Alcohol sales are responsible for between 10-15% of his sales.
However, he operates a small business on thin margins and was
concerned that if he was not able to sell alcohol, customers would
go to a nearby shop.
 
Decision
 

18)  The Panel were
aware of the options available to it. Namely whether to:

a.   
Modify the conditions of the existing License;

b.   
Exclude a licensable activity;

c.    
Suspend the License; or

d.   
Revoke the License.
 

19)  Paragraph 11.29 of
the Statutory Guidance states:
“where
persistent sales of alcohol to children have occurred at premises,
and it is apparent that those managing the premises do not operate
a responsible policy or have not exercised appropriate due
diligence, responsible authorities should consider taking steps to
ensure that a review of the licence is the norm in these
circumstances. This is particularly the case where there has been a
prosecution for the offence under section 147A or a closure notice
has been given under section 169A of the 2003 Act. In determining
the review, the licensing authority should consider revoking the
licence if it considers this appropriate.”
 

20)  After considering
all of the representations before it, the Panel had serious
concerns about the License Holder’s ability to uphold the
licensing objectives or supervise the Premises
responsibly.
 

21)  The
Panel considered the representations made about the License
Holder’s friend; that she was not a member of staff and was
not familiar with alcoholic drinks. In the Panel’s view,
neither representation was adequate to explain why a person with no
training was allowed to sell alcohol. Whether the person was
familiar with alcoholic drinks was not a valid explanation, as only
a person with adequate training should be permitted to make a sale,
as they would have knowledge of the products on offer as result of
the training.
 

22)  Additionally, the
sale in October 2025 was not the first incident of this nature at
the Premises. Despite being convicted of selling alcohol to a
person under the age of 18, adequate safeguards were not put in
place to ensure it would not happen again. This was a further
indication of the failure of supervision by the License Holder.
 

23)  The
Panel considered that allowing the Premises to continue to operate
with conditions added to the license would not be suitable due to
the changes in management which would be needed. The Panel was of
the opinion that this could not happen quickly. For the same
reason, the Panel considered that suspension of the license would
not be sufficient, as three months would not be enough time to
change the attitude of the business.
 

24)  The
Panel was sympathetic to the representation about the effect on the
business if it was not allowed to sell alcohol. However, the Panel
found that allowing an untrained person to carry out a licensable
activity was a deeply concerning breach of the licensing objectives
and indicative of a failure of supervision, and suggestive of the
business’s poor management ethos. This failure of supervision
resulted in the sale of alcohol to a child, which directly
undermines the licensing objectives. Due to these concerns, the
Panel was of the view that revocation of the license was a
proportionate measure.
 
Right to Appeal
 

25)  Any party aggrieved with the decision of the
Licensing Sub-Committee on one or more grounds set out
in schedule 5 of Licensing
Act 2003 may appeal to the local Magistrates’ Court within 21
days of notification of this decision.
topline: The Licensing Panel has decided to revoke the premises license for Trishul Groceries in Brentford due to repeated instances of selling alcohol to minors, raising concerns about the License Holder's ability to uphold licensing objectives.
